To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
prolonged afferent stimulation leads to the degeneration of dentate hilar interneurons and that this effect can be prevented by increasing the calcium binding ability of the cell.
prolonged afferent stimulation in vivo leads to a degeneration only of cells that lack immunocytochemical reactivity for calcium binding protein.
intracellular calcium accumulation leads to cell deterioration and that the calcium binding protein parvalbumin protects cells against this effect.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of neurodegeneration and neuroprotection in the brain.
the effects of long-term synaptic activation in the brain.
the effects of calcium binding proteins on neuronal function, with a special interest in their possible role in the protection of neurons from calcium-induced cell deterioration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of calcium binding proteins in a cell protects that cell from the effects of prolonged activation.
the calcium binding capacity protects the cells from damage.
the calcium-binding proteins parvalbumn and calbindin protect against the effects on neurons of afferent stimulation that is prolonged beyond physiological limits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

prolonged stimulation of the dentate gyrus leads to cell death in a subpopulation of cells that do not contain calcium binding proteins, and that this subpopulation of cells can be protected by intracellular calcium buffering.
the calcium-binding proteins parvalbumins and calbindins, in concert with the calcium-binding protein calretinin, protect against calcium overload in neurons of the dentate gyrus.

the calcium binding proteins are not only important for the regulation of intracellular calcium levels, but that they may also protect cells against damage caused by an excessive increase in intracellular free calcium levels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence or absence of calcium binding proteins can determine whether a neuron is vulnerable or protected against activity-induced cell deterioration.
the presence of a calcium binding protein in a cell is not sufficient to protect it from the consequences of prolonged afferent stimulation.
calcium binding proteins can protect cells against the effects of excessive stimulation, and that this effect is mediated through the calcium binding capacity.
